source_text: Et cum mihi referretur: non ergo sunt malae diuinationes huius modi nec deo displicent — alioquin omnipotens et iustus ista fieri non permitteret, si mala et iniusta essent — respondi non ideo haec uideri iusta debere, quod ea fieri permittit omnipotentissimus et iustissimus deus; nam et alia multa manifestissime iniuste fieri, sicut homicidia, adulteria, furta, rapinas et cetera huius modi: quae quamuis iusto deo eo quod iniusta sint sine dubitatione displiceant, idem tamen omnipotens ea fieri certa iudicii sui ratione permittit non utique inpune, sed ad eorum damnationem, a quibus fiunt quae displicent iusto.
thought_title: God permits injustice for the damnation of the doers
orientation: Augustine is answering the objection that if God permits demonic predictions, they cannot be evil or displeasing to God.
pass_a_gloss: And when [it] was reported to me: not therefore are evil divinations of this kind nor to God are they displeasing — otherwise [the] almighty and just [one] these things to happen not would permit, if evil and unjust they were — I answered not for this reason these [things] to seem just [that they] ought, because them to happen permits [the] most almighty and most just God; for also other many [things] manifestly unjustly to happen, as murders, adulteries, thefts, robberies and [the] rest of this kind: which although to [the] just God for this reason that unjust they are without doubt are displeasing, [the] same nevertheless almighty [one] them to happen by [a] certain of his judgment reason permits not indeed unpunished, but unto their condemnation, by whom are done [the things] which are displeasing to [the] just [one].

choices.english: the most almighty and most righteous God
choices.why: Keeps the superlative force of the Latin, which intensifies the interlocutors' own terms 'omnipotens et iustus' to stress that even the highest divine attributes do not make permitted acts just.
rejected: the all-powerful and most just God
the omnipotent and most righteous God

choices.english: by a sure reckoning of his judgment
choices.why: Renders 'ratio' as 'reckoning' to convey a deliberate, ordered plan rather than a mere reason; 'sure' keeps the force of 'certa' as fixed and certain.
rejected: by a certain reason of his judgment
by the sure plan of his judgment

choices.why: Preserves the emphatic 'utique' and the legal sense of 'inpune' as 'without punishment', which is central to Augustine's point that permission is not approval.

choices.term: ad eorum damnationem, a quibus fiunt
choices.english: for the damnation of those by whom are done
choices.why: Keeps the passive 'fiunt' and the relative clause structure, preserving the emphasis that the doers are the objects of damnation.
rejected: for the condemnation of those who do them
to damn those who do them

pass_b_english: And when it was reported to me: “Then divinations of this kind are not evil, and they do not displease God—otherwise the Almighty and the righteous God would not permit such things to happen, if they were evil and unjust”—I answered that these things should not for that reason be considered just, because the most almighty and most righteous God permits them to happen. For many other things are also done most manifestly unjustly, such as murders, adulteries, thefts, robberies, and others of this kind. Although these things, because they are unjust, without doubt displease the righteous God, yet the same Almighty permits them to happen by a sure reckoning of his judgment—not at all with impunity, but for the damnation of those by whom are done the things that displease the righteous God.

last_rejected.quote: most almighty and most righteous God
last_rejected.why: Superlatives flattened: 'omnipotentissimus' and 'iustissimus' mean 'most almighty' and 'most just', not merely 'most almighty and most righteous'.
last_rejected.fix: the most almighty and most just God
last_rejected.ruling: English renders both superlatives ('most almighty and most righteous'); 'iustissimus' as 'most righteous' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: those by whom are done the things that displease the righteous God
last_rejected.source_quote: a quibus fiunt quae displicent iusto
last_rejected.why: Inverted syntax 'by whom are done the things' is ungrammatical/awkward; should be 'by whom the things are done'.
last_rejected.fix: for the damnation of those by whom the things that displease the just are done.
last_rejected.ruling: 'By whom are done the things' is archaic but grammatical passive; not a major error, just stylistic awkwardness.
